records.place: Madeba farm near Robertson, Breede River Valley, Western Cape

wine.name: Graham Beck Brut
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in roughly equal parts, by the house's sheet, with reserve wine from earlier years where the blend needs it.
wine.sites: Parcels across the Western Cape blended with the house's Robertson fruit, where lime rich soils and warm days with cool nights first drew the founder.
wine.making: The Chardonnay and the Pinot Noir are fermented apart after the juice settles, then blended with reserve wine where needed, bottled for the second fermentation and left on the yeast for about a year to eighteen months, by the house's sheets, before disgorging; never a vintage on the label.
wine.glass: Lemon zest, green apple and pear with a little brioche and praline, a fine, steady mousse, brisk acidity and a clean, chalky finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink on release, while its fruit is fresh; a year or two more in bottle adds a little toast, but it gains nothing from long keeping.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass or a tulip rather than a flute.

label.means: The South African name for sparkling wine made by the second fermentation in the bottle, used since 1992.
Dry, with only a little sugar added at the dosage.
Grown in the Western Cape, so the blend may draw on districts beyond Robertson.

records.table: Graham Beck is the Robertson house given wholly to Cap Classique, and its Brut, a non vintage blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, is the bottle poured at Nelson Mandela's inauguration in 1994. Expect green apple, lemon zest and a little brioche on a brisk, fine mousse.
records.story: Graham Beck (1929 to 2010) made his fortune in coal and came to Robertson first for horses, buying a stud farm there in 1976. In 1983 he bought Madeba, a farm outside the town, drawn, as the house tells it, by lime rich soils and warm days with cool nights that recalled Champagne, and set out to make a sparkling wine of his own. The cellar was not finished in time for the first harvest of 1991, which the house says was gathered under the stars, and its maiden wine was a Blanc de Blancs of that year. The Brut, the non vintage blend, followed, and in May 1994 it was poured at the inauguration of Nelson Mandela as South Africa's first democratically elected president, which earned it the name of the President's Choice. Beck later bought Bellingham in Franschhoek and Steenberg in Constantia, and he died in London in 2010. In 2016 the house dropped its still wines to make nothing but Cap Classique. For a sommelier the Brut is the first Cap Classique a guest is likely to name: fresh, dry and made in the bottle like Champagne, but South African in every grape.

others.name: Graham Beck Blanc de Blancs
others.note: The vintage Chardonnay Cap Classique, first made in 1991 as the house's maiden wine.

others.name: Cuvée Clive
others.note: The prestige cuvée of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, made only in selected years.

others.name: Graham Beck Brut Rosé
others.note: The pink partner of the Brut, also non vintage, with Pinot Noir to the fore.

traps: Cap Classique names a method, the second fermentation in the bottle, not a region or an appellation.
The Brut carries no vintage and is labelled Western Cape; the vintage Blanc de Blancs, not the Brut, was the house's first wine of 1991.
Cap Classique asks for less time on the lees than Champagne, so never assume Champagne's minimums for a Cape bottle.

cards.front: Graham Beck Brut: at which state occasion of May 1994 was it poured?
cards.back: The inauguration of Nelson Mandela as president, which gave it the name the President's Choice.

cards.front: What did Graham Beck give up in 2016?
cards.back: Its still wines: from then the house made only Cap Classique.

questions.q: A guest asks what makes Graham Beck Brut a Cap Classique. Which answer fits?
opts: Its second fermentation takes place in the bottle
It is grown only on Robertson limestone
It is carbonated in a pressure tank
It is aged for three years in oak
questions.exp: Cap Classique is the Cape's name for the bottle fermented method; the Brut is labelled Western Cape, so it is not defined by Robertson soil alone.

questions.q: In which year did Graham Beck buy the Robertson farm Madeba to make sparkling wine?
questions.exp: Madeba was bought in 1983; 1976 was the stud farm, 1991 the first harvest and 1994 the inauguration at which the Brut was poured.

sources.title: Graham Beck: The founder, the vineyards and the Cap Classique journey
Graham Beck: Brut Non Vintage specification sheet
Wikipedia: Graham Beck
Decanter: Graham Beck dies

report: The Brut is labelled Wine of Origin Western Cape on the house's sheet and in Falstaff's listing, not Robertson; the library's holdings line reads as if all its fruit were Robertson's, so the record says the blend draws on the wider Western Cape.
The house's spec sheet gives 15 to 18 months on the yeast for the Brut while its general Cap Classique page gives 12 for the non vintage wines, so the record says about a year to eighteen months.
Sources disagree whether the inauguration wine was the non vintage Brut or a Brut of 1994; the house calls the Brut the President's Choice, and the record follows it.
The 2016 move to Cap Classique alone rests on Wine with Seth, Club Oenologique and Top Wines SA; the cellar master recalls a decision of 2014 in a Daily Maverick interview.
Bellingham and Steenberg rest on Wikipedia and the Decanter obituary; the 2008 Obama toast was left out, as sources disagree whether it marked the nomination or the election.
The cellar master since 1990 is living and is not named.

records.place: De Wetshof Estate near Robertson, Breede River Valley, Western Cape

wine.name: Bateleur Chardonnay
wine.sites: A single vineyard of the estate planted in 1987, on gravel from limestone rich mountain rock with clay, a soil of high pH, by the house's fact sheet.
wine.making: The settled juice is fermented in French oak barrels, new in the vintages whose sheets were read, then kept on its lees with weekly stirring; it is racked and returned to barrel for about twelve months in all before bottling.
wine.glass: Lemon curd and Meyer lemon over baked oats and smoked almond, with a touch of grilled pineapple and vanilla from the oak; broad and creamy, yet held by a fresh, chalky line.
wine.ageing: Open and generous on release, it gains from three or four years in bottle, and the house says it keeps for many years when well stored.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle gains from air; a Burgundy white glass.

label.means: The African eagle the wine is named for, a bird of the Robertson skies.
Grown in the Robertson district of the Breede River Valley.
Grown, made and bottled on one registered wine estate.

records.table: De Wetshof is the family estate that staked Robertson's lime soils on Chardonnay, and Bateleur, named for an African eagle, is its barrel fermented Chardonnay from a single vineyard planted in 1987. Expect lemon curd, oats and almond on a chalky line.
records.story: The De Wet family settled on the farm near Robertson in 1949. The founder's son went to Germany to study at Geisenheim, graduated in 1972 and came home to build what the sources describe as the first private cellar in the Robertson valley; De Wetshof, by its own account, became the valley's first registered wine estate. He saw in the district's calcareous soils, rare in the Cape, a home for Chardonnay, and planted and championed the grape when it was a rarity in South Africa, which the house claims as introducing it to the country. In July 1987 the vineyard that gives Bateleur was planted on gravel and lime, and its wine took the name of the bateleur, an eagle known for its gliding flight. The family has run the estate across three generations since. For a sommelier, Bateleur is the Robertson answer to Burgundy: barrel fermented Chardonnay from some of the older vines of the grape in the Cape, on the limestone that sets the district apart.

others.name: De Wetshof Limestone Hill Chardonnay
others.note: A Chardonnay of the estate named for the lime rich ground on which the farm is known.

traps: Bateleur is a Chardonnay of Robertson, inland and warm, not of the cool Cape south coast; its freshness comes from lime soils and cool nights.
De Wetshof's claim to have introduced Chardonnay to South Africa is the house's; Backsberg is also credited with an early varietal Chardonnay of 1980.

cards.front: De Wetshof Bateleur: what is the name of, and when were its vines planted?
cards.back: An African eagle; the single vineyard went in during July 1987.

cards.front: Where did the man who built De Wetshof's cellar study, and when did he graduate?

questions.q: A guest asks how De Wetshof makes its Bateleur Chardonnay. Which answer fits?
opts: Fermented in French oak barrels and kept on its lees
Fermented in steel and bottled with no oak at all
Aged for years under a veil of flor yeast
Fermented on its skins in clay amphorae
questions.exp: Bateleur is fermented and aged for about a year in French oak, new in the vintages read, with weekly stirring of the lees; it is no unwooded wine.

questions.q: In which year did the De Wet family settle on the farm that became De Wetshof?
questions.exp: The family came to the farm in 1949; 1972 is the year the cellar's builder graduated from Geisenheim and 1987 the planting of the Bateleur vineyard.

Wine with Seth: De Wetshof Estate

report: The plan's note gives no founding year; 1949, the family's arrival on the farm, rests on Wine with Seth, Meininger and the importer's biography.
The year of registration as Robertson's first estate is 1972 in one source and the late 1970s in another, so the record gives no year.
The first Bateleur vintage is 1991 in Wine with Seth alone, and the maiden estate Chardonnay of 1981 in the same source, so both are left out.
The plan names The Site as a wine beside Bateleur; I found no source for it in my share, so it is not listed in others.
The founder's son who built the cellar and his sons who run the estate are living and are not named; the founder's dates were not found, so he is described, not named.
Vine age and soils of the Bateleur vineyard rest on the producer's fact sheet as published by its importer, with the planting year of 1987 also in Wine with Seth and Winemag.

records.place: Springfield Estate near Robertson, Breede River Valley, Western Cape

wine.name: Life from Stone Sauvignon Blanc
wine.sites: A parcel of the estate so strewn with quartz that the stones had to be cleared from the surface before it could be planted; the soil is about seven tenths quartz rock, by the house's sheet.
wine.making: Picked at night under dry ice to keep the fruit cool and away from air, fermented for about three weeks, then left for about a hundred days on its primary lees and racked under carbon dioxide; bottled on the estate after only a light filtration, never sterile filtered.
wine.glass: Flint and crushed stone over gooseberry, lemon peel and green apple, concentrated and taut rather than showy, with bright acidity and a dry, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, in its first two or three years, while the fruit is fresh; a good vintage holds its line a little longer.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass.

label.means: The house's name for the wine, taken from the rocky quartz ground of its parcel.
Grown in the Robertson district of the Breede River Valley.
Grown, made and bottled on the family's own farm.

records.table: Springfield Estate is the Robertson family farm known for Sauvignon Blanc, and Life from Stone comes from a parcel so thick with quartz that the stones were cleared before planting. Expect flint, gooseberry and lemon peel, taut and dry; pour it young and cold.
records.story: The family behind Springfield traces itself, by its own account, to French Huguenots who left the Loire for the Cape in 1688, and it has farmed this land near Robertson since 1898. The estate made its name in 1995 with a Sauvignon Blanc that found a market at home and abroad. The family's way is to work in the vineyard rather than the cellar, and most of its wines ferment with the yeasts on the grape skins. Life from Stone came from one rocky parcel, so fragmented with quartz that its surface had to be cleared before planting, and the family's story is that the name came to its maker from a song on the car radio on the drive home from a trade event in Cape Town. When the first vintage came out, as Wineland tells it, critics had said such a wine was hard to make in so warm a district. Its making is reductive, kept from air from picking to bottling. For a sommelier it is Robertson Sauvignon Blanc told by its ground: flinty, taut and dry, from a parcel of quartz.

others.name: Springfield Special Cuvée Sauvignon Blanc
others.note: The estate's other Sauvignon Blanc, from a different parcel of the farm.

others.name: Springfield Wild Yeast Chardonnay
others.note: A Chardonnay fermented with the yeasts on the grape skins, as the house makes most of its wines.

others.name: Springfield Méthode Ancienne Chardonnay
others.note: A Chardonnay made by what the house calls an old method, a wine apart from the Wild Yeast.

traps: Life from Stone is the Sauvignon Blanc; Méthode Ancienne and Wild Yeast are the estate's Chardonnays, not sparkling wines.
Springfield Estate of Robertson is a different house from Bon Courage, though both families take their name from Huguenot forebears of the Loire.

cards.front: Springfield Life from Stone: why is it so named?
cards.back: Its parcel is so strewn with quartz that the stones had to be cleared before planting.

cards.front: Since when has the Springfield Estate family farmed its land near Robertson?

questions.q: A guest asks why Springfield's Life from Stone tastes of flint rather than ripe tropical fruit. Which reason fits?
opts: Quartz strewn ground and making kept away from air
Long ageing in new French oak barrels
A late harvest of shrivelled grapes
Fruit bought in from the cool south coast
questions.exp: The parcel is about seven tenths quartz rock and the wine is made reductively, picked at night and racked under carbon dioxide; it sees no new oak.

questions.q: From which French region did the Springfield family's Huguenot forebears come to the Cape in 1688?
opts: The Loire
Champagne
Burgundy
Alsace
questions.exp: The house traces its family to Huguenots of the Loire who reached the Cape in 1688; the Huguenots of the Cape came from many regions, but the house names the Loire.

sources.title: Springfield Estate: About
Springfield Estate: Life From Stone product and specification page
Decanter: PIWOSA producer profile, Springfield Estate
Wineland: Springfield's Life from Stone celebrates 21 years
Wine with Seth: Springfield Estate

report: The first vintage of Life from Stone is left out: Wineland's anniversary piece counts both 21 and 23 years back and calls the 2021 release the 22nd vintage, which do not agree; the song it names is of 1998.
The year 1995 for the estate's first acclaimed Sauvignon Blanc rests on the Decanter profile and Wine with Seth; a retailer's family run since 1957 was not used.
The generation count differs between sources (fourth and ninth generation), so none is given; the siblings who run the estate are living and are not named.
Gooseberry rests on one Norwegian tasting note; flint and a mineral concentration are in several, so the glass leans on those.
The Méthode Ancienne note is deliberately general: I did not source how it is made.

records.place: Rietvallei Wine Estate near Robertson, Breede River Valley, Western Cape

wine.name: Rietvallei 1908 Muscadel
wine.grapes: Red Muscadel, the red skinned Muscat de Frontignan, all of it.
wine.sites: A block of bush vines planted on the estate in 1908, which the house calls the oldest Red Muscadel vineyard in South Africa; the old vines give very low yields of concentrated fruit.
wine.making: Picked by hand very ripe, lightly crushed and kept on the skins for two days, the mash worked every couple of hours; fortified with wine spirit, left on its lees for about six months, then racked into older French oak barrels of 500 litres for well over a year on the fine lees, by the house's sheet for 2021.
wine.glass: Deep red; a perfumed, grapey Muscat nose of raisin and fresh grape, full bodied, rich and very sweet, kept lively by tangy acidity and the warmth of the spirit.
wine.ageing: Ready on release after its time in barrel; its sugar and spirit let it keep for many years in bottle.
wine.serve: Lightly chilled, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a small white wine glass and a small measure.

label.means: The year the vineyard was planted, never a vintage; the vintage is printed apart.
The Cape name for Muscat de Frontignan and its fortified sweet wine.
Grown in the Robertson district of the Breede River Valley.

records.table: Rietvallei is the Burger family's Robertson estate since 1864, and its 1908 Muscadel is a fortified Red Muscadel from bush vines planted in that year, aged in old French oak. Expect raisin and a grapey Muscat perfume; pour it lightly chilled in a small glass.
records.story: In 1864 a member of the Burger family bought Rietvallei, a farm in the Robertson valley, for his son, and the estate has passed down the family ever since, which makes it one of the older family wine farms of the Cape. In 1908 that son, by then seventy years old by the house's account, planted a small vineyard of Red Muscadel as bush vines on the farm. For most of the century that followed Rietvallei sold its grapes and wine to others; by the house's account its first estate bottled wine came in 1975, and fittingly it was a Rooi Muskadel, a Red Muscadel. A new generation took up the reins in 2002. The old block's wine is named for the year of its planting: picked very ripe, kept on its skins for colour, fortified with spirit and aged in old French oak. The house says it follows the family's own recipe, handed down since 1864, and calls the vineyard the oldest of its kind in the country. For a sommelier the 1908 Muscadel is the Cape's fortified Muscat at its most historic: a living vineyard older than the Union of South Africa, made into a sweet wine to sip slowly.

others.name: Rietvallei Red Muscadel
others.note: The estate's younger Red Muscadel, fortified as soon as the must is pressed off the skins and bottled after a few months on its fine lees.

traps: The 1908 on the label is the year the vines were planted, not the vintage of the wine.
The 1908 Muscadel is a fortified wine, sweet from grape sugar kept by the spirit, not a late harvest or a Noble Late Harvest.

cards.front: Rietvallei 1908 Muscadel: what does the 1908 on its label mean?
cards.back: The year its bush vines of Red Muscadel were planted on the estate.

cards.front: In which year did the Burger family buy Rietvallei?
cards.back: In 1864, bought for the buyer's son.

questions.q: A guest asks how Rietvallei's 1908 Muscadel gets its deep red colour. Which answer fits?
opts: Two days on the skins of a red skinned Muscat
A blend with Pinotage after fortification
Long ageing in new charred barrels
Grapes dried on mats in the sun
questions.exp: The red skinned Muscat de Frontignan stays on its skins for two days before fortification; the barrels are old French oak, not new, and no other grape is added.

questions.q: By the house's account, what was Rietvallei's first estate bottled wine, in 1975?
opts: A Red Muscadel
A Chardonnay
A Cap Classique
A Cabernet Franc
questions.exp: The house dates its first bottling to 1975, a Rooi Muskadel, the Red Muscadel; its Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc came later.

sources.title: Rietvallei Wine Estate: Our heritage
Rietvallei Wine Estate: 1908 Muscadel 2021 product page
wine.co.za: Rietvallei Estate history and 1908 Red Muscadel listings
Wikipedia: Rietvallei Wine Estate
Winemag: Rietvallei 1908 Muscadel 2013

report: The buyer of 1864 and his son, who planted the vineyard, are described, not named: their birth and death dates were not found; the son's age of seventy is the house's, repeated by wine.co.za, its own listing.
The claim of the oldest Red Muscadel vineyard in South Africa is hedged as the house's; Wikipedia marks it citation needed.
The block's size is left out as the plan asks; the leaders of 1975 and 2002 are not named, being of living generations or undated.
The first vintage bottled as the 1908 Muscadel was not found, so the story gives none; the winemaker who took over in 2002 is living and is not named.
One wine.co.za listing gives a 2013 bottle as Muscat d'Alexandrie, against the Muscat de Frontignan of every other listing; the record follows the house and the majority.
The label term 1908 Muscadel is the house's; wine.co.za lists it as 1908 Red Muscadel.

records.place: Bon Courage Estate on the Breede River near Robertson, Western Cape

wine.name: Jacques Bruére Brut Reserve
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir, the larger part, with Chardonnay for the rest.
wine.sites: Robertson fruit, from the district where the Klaas Voogds River joins the Breede and the estate's vines grow on the valley's lime rich soils.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method throughout: the base wine rests on its lees for about eight months, then goes to bottle for its second fermentation and stays on the yeast for four to five years before disgorging, by the house's sheets; a vintage is printed on the label.
wine.glass: Peach, lemon and grapefruit pith over brioche and a buttery creaminess, with a very fine mousse and poised acidity; the Pinot Noir gives it a gentle generosity.
wine.ageing: Released only after years on its yeast and ready to drink then; it holds well for five years or so after release.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass or a tulip rather than a flute.

label.means: The range named for the family's Huguenot forebears, the Bruéres of the Loire.
South African sparkling wine made by the second fermentation in the bottle.
The dry blend of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay at the head of the range.

records.table: Bon Courage is the Bruwer family's estate on the Breede River, and its Jacques Bruére Brut Reserve is a vintage Cap Classique of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay left four to five years on its yeast. Expect peach, grapefruit and brioche over a creamy, very fine mousse.
records.story: The Bruwer family traces its wine farming, by its own account, to French Huguenot forebears, the Bruéres, who grew vines in the Loire before they left France for the Cape. Their Robertson chapter began in 1927, when the family's patriarch bought the farm Goedemoed from the local Dutch Reformed Church; its Cape Dutch homestead dates from 1818. In October 1983 his son renamed the farm Bon Courage, the French for Goedemoed, in honour of those forebears, and registered it as a wine estate, and the family began to sell its own wines. In time the estate gave its Cap Classique the old French form of the family name, Jacques Bruére, for a range of three: the Brut Reserve, a Blanc de Blancs and a Cuvée Rosé Brut, each made by hand in the traditional way and kept on the yeast for years before release. A rosé of 2006 shows the range was established by then. For a sommelier the Brut Reserve is Robertson's second voice in Cap Classique beside Graham Beck: a vintage wine, longer on its lees than most, from a family estate where the Klaas Voogds River meets the Breede.

others.name: Jacques Bruére Blanc de Blancs
others.note: The all Chardonnay vintage Cap Classique of the range, kept on its yeast for longer again.

others.name: Jacques Bruére Cuvée Rosé Brut
others.note: The rosé of the range, a vintage Cap Classique released by 2006.

traps: Jacques Bruére names the Cap Classique range of Bon Courage, not a separate house or a person who founded the estate.
Unlike the Graham Beck Brut, the Jacques Bruére Brut Reserve is a vintage wine, with several years on its yeast.

cards.front: Bon Courage Jacques Bruére: for whom is the range named?
cards.back: The Bruwer family's Huguenot forebears, the Bruéres of the Loire.

cards.front: Bon Courage: what was the farm called before October 1983?
cards.back: Goedemoed, of which Bon Courage is the French translation.

questions.q: A guest asks how long Bon Courage keeps its Jacques Bruére Brut Reserve on the yeast. Which answer fits?
opts: Four to five years before disgorging
Nine months, the Cap Classique minimum
Fifteen months, as for non vintage Champagne
No time at all, as it is tank made
questions.exp: The house's sheets give 48 to 60 months on the yeast after the second fermentation in bottle; it is made by the traditional method, never in tank.

questions.q: From whom did the Bruwer family buy the farm Goedemoed in 1927?
opts: The local Dutch Reformed Church
The Dutch East India Company
A Stellenbosch co-operative
A Huguenot family of Franschhoek
questions.exp: The family's patriarch bought Goedemoed from the Dutch Reformed Church in 1927; the Huguenot link is the family's ancestry, not the seller.

sources.title: Bon Courage Estate: Jacque Bruére range page
Bon Courage Estate: Jacques Bruére Brut Reserve 2012 technical sheet
wine.co.za: Bon Courage Estate history
Decanter: Bon Courage Jacques Bruére Brut Reserve 2014 review
Wine with Seth: Bon Courage Estate

report: The label spelling Jacques Bruére is confirmed by the house's sheets and Decanter, though the house's range page is addressed jacque-bruere; the Brut Reserve leads the house's list of the three, so the pick stands and no swap to Weltevrede is proposed.
The house says the range honours its Huguenot forebears; the estate's cellar master, a living member of the family, shares the first name, and the record names no living person.
The patriarch of 1927 and his son of 1983, the latter dead by a wine.co.za tribute, are described, not named, for want of dates in two sources.
The first vintage of the range was not found; the record says only that a rosé of 2006 shows it was established by then (wine.co.za news).

The grapes follow the 2012 sheet and Decanter (Pinot Noir about three fifths); that the Brut Reserve is wholly estate grown was not confirmed, so the sites line names the district and the estate's setting only.
The ageing window rests on Decanter's drinking window for the 2014 and is the softest line of the wine fields.
